title: The tools that find memory bugs for you
objective: By the end of this lesson you can run the three kinds of tool that catch memory defects, read their reports fluently, and put them where they run automatically instead of when you remember.

blocks.text: C does not check memory access at runtime, which is why it is fast. The tools in this lesson add those checks back when you ask for them. Learning to read their output is one of the highest-return skills in the language — most memory bugs stop being mysteries the moment one of these is running.
Three kinds of tool, three different jobs

rows: Suspicious code, format mismatches, obvious mistakes

blocks.text: Warnings first, because they are free

blocks.caption: The set worth using everywhere
lines: # -Wshadow         a local variable hiding another one
# -Wconversion     implicit conversions that may lose data
# -Werror          make them all errors — the right default for a shared project

blocks.title: A warning you ignore is worse than no warning
blocks.text: Once a build prints twenty warnings, nobody reads the twenty-first — and that is the one that mattered. Fix them to zero, then add -Werror so the count cannot creep back up. A clean build is what makes a new warning meaningful.
AddressSanitizer: the one to reach for first

blocks.caption: Build and run
lines: # Leak reporting is on by default on Linux; enable it explicitly if needed:

blocks.caption: Reading a report from the top
lines: READ of size 4 at 0x602000000010 thread T0
#0 0x55d1 in process items.c:42          <- where the bad access happened
0x602000000010 is located 0 bytes inside of 40-byte region
#1 0x55c9 in cleanup items.c:31          <- where it was freed
previously allocated by thread T0 here:
#2 0x55b2 in create items.c:18           <- where it came from

blocks.text: Three locations: where it broke, where the memory was released, and where it was created. That is usually the whole investigation. Read them in that order and the fix is normally obvious by the third line.

rows: Out-of-bounds on heap, stack and globals; use-after-free; double free. With Clang, add -fsanitize-address-use-after-return=always for guaranteed use-after-return instrumentation; leak detection depends on platform and runtime configuration
Signed overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned access, division by zero, bad casts
Data races between threads — cannot be combined with address
Reads of uninitialised memory (Clang; requires all code instrumented)

blocks.title: Never ship a sanitizer build
blocks.text: They roughly double memory use and runtime, and their error handlers are diagnostic aids, not security boundaries. Sanitizers belong in development and CI. Production builds use -O2 with warnings clean and, where the platform offers them, hardening options such as stack protection and fortified library calls.

blocks.caption: No instrumentation required
lines: # ==3021==  Address 0x4a4b050 is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd
# Slower than the sanitizers, but works on an existing binary
# and catches uninitialised reads that AddressSanitizer does not.

blocks.caption: The CI step that keeps this honest
lines: # non-zero; without it, a UBSan diagnostic may still exit successfully.

blocks.title: A tool you run when you remember is a tool that does not run
blocks.text: The value of these checks is not that they exist but that they run on every change, on a machine nobody configured specially. That is the same argument as the CI lesson in the Git course, applied to the class of defect C is most known for.

blocks.title: Run all three against the same bug
steps: Write a program with a heap overflow: char *p = malloc(8); p[10] = 'x';
Read all three locations in the report
Run: valgrind ./prog     (if installed) and compare the two reports
Add a leak and confirm the sanitizer reports it at exit
Add -Werror to the build and fix everything until it is clean
Write the CI step above into a workflow file
blocks.expected: The same defect: invisible in a normal build, named precisely by the sanitizer with three locations, described differently by Valgrind, and finally caught automatically by a CI step you wrote. That progression is the working method for C.

cheatsheet: Warnings are free: -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow -Wconversion, and -Werror on shared code
Fix warnings to zero, or the important one gets lost in the noise
-fsanitize=address finds out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free, and leaks
-fsanitize=undefined finds signed overflow, bad shifts, and misalignment
Combine address and undefined; thread cannot be combined with address
Read a report as three locations: where it broke, where it was freed, where it was allocated
Valgrind needs no rebuild and catches uninitialised reads, but is much slower
Never ship a sanitizer build — they are diagnostics, not protections
Put the sanitizer build in CI so the check runs without anyone remembering

checkpoint.prompt: What are the three locations in an AddressSanitizer use-after-free report?

choices.A: The compiler, the linker, and the program loader
choices.B: Where it happened, was freed, and was allocated
choices.D: The stack, the heap, and the globals

checkpoint.explanation: The three locations are where the invalid access happened, where the memory was freed, and where it was allocated. Those three lines usually contain the entire investigation. Read them in order and the fix is normally clear immediately.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should a sanitizer build never be shipped to production?

choices.A: It cannot be compiled with -O2 at all
choices.D: It roughly doubles runtime and memory

checkpoint.explanation: Its checks are diagnostic aids rather than security boundaries. Use sanitizers in development and CI. For production, use a clean warning-free build plus the platform's hardening options.

checkpoint.prompt: When is Valgrind the better choice over a sanitizer?

choices.B: When the program is very large and slow to start
choices.C: When you cannot rebuild the binary
choices.D: When you only care about leaks

checkpoint.explanation: Or when you need uninitialised-read detection that AddressSanitizer does not provide. It works on an existing binary and covers a case the address sanitizer does not, at the cost of running much more slowly.

checkpoint.prompt: Why put the sanitizer build in CI rather than running it when you suspect a problem?

choices.A: A check that needs remembering does not run
choices.B: It replaces the need for tests
choices.D: It always runs faster on the CI machines themselves

checkpoint.explanation: In CI it runs on every change and blocks the merge when it reports something. The same argument as any other automated check: the value comes from it running without anyone deciding to run it.
